title: Paul Before King Agrippa
summary: Given permission to speak, Paul tells King Agrippa the story of his life: his strict upbringing as a Pharisee, his violent persecution of Jesus's followers, and his encounter with the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus, who sent him to the Gentiles. When Paul declares that Moses and the prophets foretold a suffering and risen Christ, Festus calls him mad, and Agrippa deflects Paul's direct appeal. The officials agree that Paul has done nothing deserving death or prison.
story: This is the last and fullest of Paul's defense speeches in Acts, and the third telling of his conversion (after Acts 9 and 22). Festus has arranged the hearing to learn what to write to the emperor (25:26-27), but Paul turns it into testimony. Jesus had told his disciples they would be brought before kings and governors for his name's sake (Luke 21:12), and the Lord had said Paul would carry his name before Gentiles and kings (Acts 9:15). Here that word is fulfilled before a Jewish king, a Roman governor, and the leading men of Caesarea. The chapter closes the Caesarea section with a verdict of innocence and a strange irony: Paul could have gone free if he had not appealed to Caesar. Now nothing stands between him and the voyage to Rome.
historical:
Agrippa II was a descendant of Herod the Great, raised partly in Rome, and he was the best informed about Judaism of any official Paul faced. Rome had given him charge of the temple's affairs, and he knew the Scriptures and the disputes of the sects. That is why Paul says he is fortunate to make his defense before him, and why Paul can say that none of the events surrounding Jesus had escaped the king's notice. The crucifixion of Jesus, the growth of the Jerusalem church, and the conflicts over it had taken place in public, in the city where Agrippa's family had long been prominent.

Paul's account of his earlier life adds details not found elsewhere: that he cast his vote against believers when they were condemned to death, that he tried to force them to blaspheme, and that he pursued them to foreign cities. Scholars debate whether casting a vote means Paul was a formal member of the Sanhedrin or is a figure of speech for approving their deaths, as he did at Stephen's stoning (Acts 8:1). Luke does not say.
cultural:
Paul speaks in the manner of a formal defense before a distinguished audience, stretching out his hand in the orator's gesture and opening with a courteous address to the king. His Greek in this speech is among the most polished in Acts, suited to the setting. The line the risen Jesus speaks to him, that it is hard to kick against the goads, echoes a proverb known in Greek literature. A goad was a pointed stick used to drive oxen; an ox that kicked back only hurt itself. The saying pictured a person resisting a divine power he could not escape.

Festus's outburst reflects a Roman gentleman's reaction to talk of a man rising from the dead. Educated Greeks and Romans often thought of the soul's survival as possible but regarded bodily resurrection as absurd (compare the mockery in Athens, Acts 17:32). To Festus, Paul's learning had tipped into madness. Agrippa's reply uses the word Christian, which appears only three times in the New Testament (here, Acts 11:26, and 1 Peter 4:16). It seems to have begun as outsiders' label for Christ's followers.
literary: The speech is a carefully shaped autobiography in three stages: Paul's life as a Pharisee (verses 4-8), his life as a persecutor (verses 9-11), and his commission by the risen Jesus (verses 12-18), followed by his obedience to it (verses 19-23). Compared with Acts 9 and 22, this version compresses the story: Ananias is not mentioned, and Jesus's commission to Paul is given in one continuous speech. The commission gathers language from the servant passages of Isaiah, the call to open blind eyes and bring light to the nations (Isaiah 42:6-7, 49:6), so that Paul presents his mission as Israel's own prophetic calling. The speech is interrupted before it can conclude, as several of Paul's speeches are, and the closing exchange with Agrippa is quick and personal.

outline.t: A Pharisee on trial for Israel's hope
The risen Jesus meets Paul and sends him
Paul's obedience and the message of the prophets
Festus's interruption and Paul's appeal to Agrippa
The verdict: nothing worthy of death

doctrines.note: Paul summarizes his preaching as a call to repent, turn to God, and perform deeds worthy of repentance. Turning from darkness to light is a change of allegiance that shows itself in how a person lives.

Jesus sends Paul so that people may receive forgiveness of sins and an inheritance among those sanctified by faith in him. Forgiveness and a place among God's people are received through faith in Christ.
Paul's commission is to Jew and Gentile alike, to open eyes and bring light. Paul presents this as the fulfillment of Moses and the prophets, not a departure from them.
Paul calls his gospel the hope of the promise made to the fathers, for which the twelve tribes worship day and night, and he asks why anyone should think it incredible that God raises the dead.

words.note: Kentron, goad or sting. It named the sharp point used to drive animals and also the sting of an insect; Paul uses it of death's sting in 1 Corinthians 15:55-56. In the proverb, Saul is pictured as fighting against the very God who was driving him.

Optasia, vision. Paul calls his Damascus experience a heavenly vision, but he treats it as a real appearance of the risen Jesus (1 Corinthians 15:8), not an inner impression. The word emphasizes that it came from heaven, not from his own mind.
Metanoia, repentance, a change of mind that turns a whole life around. In the New Testament it is more than regret. Paul's call to deeds worthy of repentance echoes John the Baptist (Luke 3:8).

Psephos, a small stone, used in the ancient world for voting. Paul says he cast his vote against believers. Whether literal or figurative, it shows how fully he shared responsibility for their deaths, which makes the grace he received the more striking.

christ: Paul's defense is really a testimony to what Jesus is. The Jesus of Nazareth whose name Paul opposed is the one who spoke from heaven in a light brighter than the noon sun, called himself by name, and identified himself with his persecuted followers: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.” He is alive, he commissions, and he forgives. Paul sums up the Scriptures' witness in verse 23: the Christ would suffer, would be the first to rise from the dead, and would proclaim light to Israel and the nations. Suffering first, then resurrection, then light to the world: that is the shape of the gospel Luke has told from the beginning of his Gospel, where old Simeon called the infant Jesus a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32).

hard.q: Why does this account of Paul's conversion differ from the ones in Acts 9 and 22?
hard.a:
The three accounts differ in details. In Acts 9 Paul's companions hear a voice but see no one; in Acts 22 they see the light but do not understand the voice; here they all fall to the ground. In the earlier accounts Jesus's commission comes through Ananias in Damascus; here Paul reports it as Jesus's own words on the road.

Most interpreters see these as the ordinary variation of a story told three times for three audiences, and note that Luke, who wrote all three, clearly did not think them contradictory. In Acts 9 the narrator tells the story; in Acts 22 Paul speaks to a Jerusalem crowd and stresses his Jewish credentials and Ananias's piety; here he speaks to a king and compresses the story to its core, the commission that came ultimately from Jesus even if Ananias delivered part of it. On hearing and understanding, the Greek verb for hear can mean either perceiving a sound or understanding speech, which many think explains the difference. Some critical scholars take the variations as signs of Luke's literary freedom with his sources. Either way, the central claims are the same in all three.

questions: Paul tells his story honestly, including the violence he once did. How can an honest account of our past make testimony more believable rather than less?
Festus thought resurrection was madness, and Agrippa kept the question at arm's length. Which of those responses is closer to your own instinct, and why?
Paul wished that everyone listening might become what he was, except for the chains. What does it look like to want good for people who hold power over you?
